text:
Education in Nigeria spans a structured system from primary to tertiary education, with a strong emphasis on compulsory and free education under the Universal Basic Education (UBE) program. Primary education lasts six years, starting at age five, covering core subjects like mathematics, English, and indigenous languages. The curriculum is free, and enrollment is compulsory for all children aged 6–14. Secondary education follows a 6-3-3-4 system, with three years of Junior Secondary School (JSS) and three years of Senior Secondary School (SSS), culminating in the Senior Secondary Certificate Examination (SSCE). Students can also pursue vocational training through technical colleges.
Federal, state, and private schools operate under different funding models, with federal schools offering lower tuition fees and state schools often requiring additional costs for books and supplies. Private schools, though expensive, provide modern facilities and better teacher qualifications. The education system is highly centralized, with the Universal Basic Education Commission (UBEC) overseeing implementation. Challenges include underfunding, teacher shortages, and disparities in educational quality, particularly in rural areas.
Tertiary education includes universities, polytechnics, and colleges of education, with public institutions receiving majority funding. Admission to universities typically requires passing the Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB) exam, with direct entry options for those with relevant qualifications. The system faces issues such as high dropout rates, limited vocational training opportunities, and regional disparities in access to quality education. Despite these challenges, Nigeria’s education system aims to provide foundational learning and prepare students for further education or employment.
